concept.name: Law of cause and effect
concept.definition: Wyckoff's second law: the horizontal extent of accumulation or distribution within a trading range (the 'cause') is related to the distance of the subsequent trend out of that range (the 'effect'), allowing price objectives to be projected from point-and-figure counts. It is a heuristic projection technique, not a deterministic relationship.
concept.intuition: The longer and harder you compress the spring inside a range, the further price travels when it's released.
concept.mechanics: The cause is measured by counting columns horizontally across a point-and-figure chart of the trading range (anchored at the LPS or count line); multiplying the column count by the box size and reversal criterion yields the projected effect, added to the count line, the range low, and their midpoint to produce a target zone.
concept.formula: Effect ≈ n x B x R, where n = number of P&F columns at the count line, B = box size, R = reversal criterion (e.g. 3); price target zone = count-line level, range low, and their midpoint, each plus (for markup) or minus (for markdown) the effect.
concept.failure_modes: Column counts are sensitive to box size and to subjective choices of where the range and count line begin and end; some moves fall well short of or far exceed their projections, so targets are zones of caution, not certainties.
concept.misconceptions: The projected target is not a promised destination; Wyckoff teaching explicitly says counts should be treated as 'stop, look and listen' points rather than exact turning levels.
concept.example: A 20-column count on a 1-point, 3-box-reversal P&F chart of a base gives a 60-point effect; added to the count line at 100, the analyst watches the 160 area for the trend to pause or end.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
